newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Economists cut forecast for Singapore growth.
newsitem.headline: Economists cut forecast for Singapore growth.

text.p: The global slowdown in demand for electronics is having a far more dramatic impact on the Singapore economy than first expected, a Reuters poll of leading financial institutions shows.

The poll of 12 economists, carried out at the end of last week, predicted Singapore's gross domestic product (GDP) would grow by just 6.5 percent this year, compared with 8.8 percent in 1995 and 10.2 percent in 1994.
The forecast is 0.6 percentage points lower than the result of a similar poll carried out by Reuters only last month.
The latest poll cut the forecast for Singapore's growth in 1997 to 7.0 percent, from 7.2 percent in last month's poll.

Almost all economists polled said they had revised down their forecasts over the last month as a result of the slump in demand for electronics and related components, on which Singapore is heavily dependent.
This sector accounts for about half the island's industrial production and almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
"Singapore is in the middle of a cyclical downturn which occurs every four or five years," said P.K. Basu, regional economist at UBS in Singapore.
"Global electronics orders are down sharply year-on-year. Consequently, we will see very weak export figures until at least the first quarter of 1997," he said.
The effects of the electronics downturn were hardly noticed during the first half of the year.
Singapore's GDP grew by a healthy 10.9 percent year-on-year in the first quarter and by 7.0 percent in the second.

But alarm bells began ringing in July when the government announced the city-state's non-oil exports had fallen by 6.1 percent year-on-year in nominal terms in June. After a rebound in July, exports slumped another 6.3 percent in August.
Economists now think Singapore's growth in the third quarter will average 3.5 percent year-on-year, according to the latest poll, down from 4.9 percent in the previous Reuters poll.
Growth in the fourth quarter was expected to average 4.9 percent, down from 6.1 percent.
Most economists said they might consider revising their forecasts further if Singapore latest trade data for September, due to be published on Monday, were much better or worse than expected.
A Reuters poll of economists on Thursday predicted Singapore would report a fall of 3.4 percent in the city-state's non-oil exports for September.

"If the export figures are much better than expected, we could revise our forecast up for the third quarter. That would push the figure for the year up as well," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS in Singapore.
"If they are worse, then we'll also have to reconsider."

Economists said they expected the Singapore government, which recently restated its prediction of seven to eight percent growth in 1996, to announce soon a downward revision of its own official forecast.
